entries.title: Leven of the Curved Workers
entries.body:
Leven’s murals use simple forms so viewers across the quay can recognize load-bearing postures. Patrons call the workers interchangeable. She adds tool marks specific to each trade, insisting that public clarity need not erase the skill of the people represented.

Later accounts make Leven of the Curved Workers the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Empty Cloth Negotiations. After several seasons of falling prices in 1123, Talassar merchants reduced wages while their stored obligations retained old values. A mural painter simplified laboring figures into bright curved forms visible across crowded quays. A public reader investigated a councilor’s splendid house and found that its builder also received favorable canal contracts. The reader lost her sponsored platform but continued recitations in market yards. Negotiators began carrying plain cloth to request safe passage, although some courts treated the sign as surrender and others as a request to speak. Confusion allowed creditors to seize people approaching in good faith. Shared standards emerged slowly from recorded incidents rather than a single heroic proclamation.

In the connected record, [The Reader’s Unsponsored Yard](b012-the-reader-s-unsponsored-yard.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Approach Without Submission](b012-the-approach-without-submission.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: how negotiated access and old debts can be revised while households still need the contracts maintaining their canals.

entries.title: The Reader’s Unsponsored Yard
entries.body:
After losing her covered platform, a reader continued beside a cooper’s yard. Rain damaged copies and reduced audiences. Neighbors supplied roofing without editorial control, creating a smaller but more dependable support than the official sponsorship she had lost.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Falling Price Houses
entries.body:
These counting houses insist lower commodity prices prove prosperity, although workers’ fixed debts now consume larger shares of income. Their account books support both observations. The conflict concerns distribution and old obligations, not merely whether one broad description of the period is correct.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The House Contract Disclosure
entries.body:
A reader linked the councilor’s home repairs to canal awards through matching wood marks and delivery dates. Officials challenged her tone instead of the records. Later inquiry confirmed favorable treatment but left the councilor’s descendants occupying the improved house.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The First Empty Cloth
entries.body:
The cloth carries no heraldic mark and began as a request for conversation. One court filed it as submission. The claimant’s surviving petition specifies safe approach without concession, preserving a distinction that would determine whether later negotiators could risk entering the gate.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Sign Explained Aloud
entries.body:
Negotiators state the cloth’s intended meaning before crossing a boundary. The receiving guard repeats it before witnesses. This cumbersome custom prevents assumptions becoming convenient evidence and makes safe approach depend upon a recorded exchange rather than a universally understood symbol.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Price of the Same Basket
entries.body:
This comparison follows one basket of food, one week’s earnings, and one inherited payment over twenty seasons. Its narrow measures challenge sweeping claims of abundance or collapse. Households use it to propose actual adjustments rather than quarrel over the period’s name.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Quay Paint Crab
entries.body:
Tiny crabs scrape mineral pigment spilled below mural walls. Their shells change hue temporarily. Festival sellers display them as living ancestral signatures, prompting the painter to demand cleaner work practices instead of treating contaminated animals as attractive proof of inspiration.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Plain Cloth Landing
entries.body:
This landing admits recognized negotiators without charging a creditor’s toll. It remains outside the debt courts’ preferred approach. Porters maintain it through small contributions, giving distressed households a physical route to talks the formal system claims to welcome.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Approach Without Submission
entries.body:
The rule separates requesting conversation from accepting judgment. Guards must record the visitor’s purpose. Creditors oppose it because it limits seizures at the gate, revealing how a supposedly neutral misunderstanding had supplied them with a profitable advantage.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Cloth Gate Seizures
entries.body:
Several debtors were seized while carrying negotiation cloths. Guards recorded no arms but entered submission on the rolls. Correcting those records released some heirs from added fees, showing that an administrative description can continue a wrong long after the immediate capture.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Mural’s Repair Patch
entries.body:
A repaired section uses cheaper pigment after sponsorship ended. Viewers initially called it artistic decline. The patch records the painter’s changed resources and the neighborhood’s continued work, making variation evidence of survival rather than a defect to conceal.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Public Contract Supper
entries.body:
Officials attending must explain one maintenance contract before eating. Some refuse the invitation as disrespectful. Contractors who accept discover questions about supplies and labor that their formal tenders never ask, widening oversight beyond literate patrons.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Dismissed Reader’s Copies
entries.body:
Independent copies preserve corrections beside the initial report. Hostile readers quote only corrected mistakes. Supporters sometimes remove the corrections. Cera insists they remain visible, because a dependable account must show how it changed when better evidence arrived.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Cloth That Stays Wet
entries.body:
One negotiation cloth remains damp after a debtor’s release despite dry storage. Its fibers contain unusual salt, which explains part of the effect. Custodians also find an unresolved undertaking to provide shelter, leaving a finite claim still requiring action.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Contract Timber Marking
entries.body:
Suppliers mark beams before delivery and retain matching cut-offs. Those ordinary practices enabled the house investigation. New officials seek standardized royal stamps, while craftsmen argue that independent marks provide evidence precisely because no one authority controls every copy.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Old Debt Price Review
entries.body:
Workers seek payments measured against current food costs. Creditors invoke authentic old undertakings. The hearing considers finite substitutions and compensated releases, requiring more practical work than declaring either inheritance sacred or every old promise meaningless.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
